question:
Of the New Zealand political parties that got more than 10,000 party votes in the 2017 General Election, find the parties that were listed as parliamentary parties in the 54th New Zealand Parliament in 2023 (according to parliament.nz) and that did not receive any party loans exceeding $30,000 in 2023 (according to Elections.nz).

 Finally, extract the parties from those found above that received list seats in the 2023 General Election and also had no successful candidates with a Wellington Central Electorate Seat in the 2023 General elections, using information from electionresults.govt.nz.

The **2017 New Zealand general election** took place on Saturday 23 September 2017 to determine the membership of the [52nd New Zealand Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/52nd_New_Zealand_Parliament "52nd New Zealand Parliament"). The [previous parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/51st_New_Zealand_Parliament "51st New Zealand Parliament") was elected on 20 September 2014 and was officially dissolved on 22 August 2017.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-1) Voters elected 120 members to the House of Representatives under New Zealand's [mixed-member proportional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed-member_proportional_representation "Mixed-member proportional representation") (MMP) voting system, a [proportional representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proportional_representation "Proportional representation") system in which 71 members were elected from single-member [electorates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_electorates "New Zealand electorates") and 49 members were elected from [closed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed_list "Closed list")[party lists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Party_list "Party list"). Around 3.57 million people were registered to vote in the election,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-2) with 2.63 million (79.8%) turning out.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-3)[Advance voting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_voting "Early voting") proved popular, with 1.24 million votes cast before election day, more than the previous two elections combined.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-5)

Prior to the election, the centre-right [National Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_National_Party "New Zealand National Party"), led by Prime Minister [Bill English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_English "Bill English"), had [governed since 2008](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fifth_National_Government_of_New_Zealand "Fifth National Government of New Zealand") in a [minority government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minority_government "Minority government") with [confidence and supply](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confidence_and_supply "Confidence and supply") from the [Māori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C4%81ori_Party "Māori Party"), [ACT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACT_New_Zealand "ACT New Zealand") and [United Future](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Future "United Future") parties. It was the first election for English as incumbent prime minister, having replaced [John Key](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Key "John Key") on 12 December 2016 and the first since [1975](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1975_New_Zealand_general_election "1975 New Zealand general election") where both major parties had leadership changes. The main opposition parties to the National government were [Labour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party "New Zealand Labour Party") (the [official opposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_Opposition_(New_Zealand) "Official Opposition (New Zealand)")), led by [Jacinda Ardern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacinda_Ardern "Jacinda Ardern"), the [Green Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Party_of_Aotearoa_New_Zealand "Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand"), and [New Zealand First](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_First "New Zealand First").

The National Party won a [plurality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plurality_(voting) "Plurality (voting)") of the seats with 56, down from 60 in 2014.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-6) Labour made large gains following Jacinda Ardern [becoming the party leader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_Labour_Party_leadership_election "2017 New Zealand Labour Party leadership election") seven weeks prior to the election, increasing its representation from 32 to 46 seats. Labour was the only parliamentary party to gain support but a large portion came at the expense of the Green Party, which lost almost half its seats (dropping from 14 to 8) following co-leader [Metiria Turei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metiria_Turei "Metiria Turei")'s resignation over self-admitted prior welfare benefit and electoral fraud. The anti-immigration populist party New Zealand First won 9 seats, down from 12 in 2014. ACT retained its one seat. Election-night counts had National with 58 seats, Labour with 45 seats, and the Greens with 7 seats, but when [special votes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_vote "Special vote") were counted, National lost one list seat each to the Greens and Labour.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-8)

The election saw five parties return to Parliament, down from seven in 2014 and the lowest number since the introduction of MMP in 1996. [Māori Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C4%81ori_Party "Māori Party") co-leader [Te Ururoa Flavell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Te_Ururoa_Flavell "Te Ururoa Flavell") lost his seat of [Waiariki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waiariki_(New_Zealand_electorate) "Waiariki (New Zealand electorate)") and, with the party's vote count being below the [threshold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_threshold "Electoral threshold") of 5%, they also lost their list MP, co-leader [Marama Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marama_Fox "Marama Fox"), and departed Parliament. [United Future](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Future "United Future") leader and sole MP [Peter Dunne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Dunne "Peter Dunne") retired from politics during the campaign due to poor polling in his electorate of [Ōhāriu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C5%8Ch%C4%81riu "Ōhāriu") and his successor failed to win the seat. The party voted to dissolve less than two months later.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-9)

Even with support partner ACT retaining its sole seat, the existing National minority government were short of the 61 seats needed to govern, and Bill English declared that the arrangement would not be continued.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-StuffNZ-negotiations-10) New Zealand First's nine seats gave it the [balance of power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balance_of_power_(parliament) "Balance of power (parliament)") between the National Party and the Labour–Green bloc.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-OfficialResults-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-ABC-FinalTally-12) On 19 October 2017, New Zealand First leader [Winston Peters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winston_Peters "Winston Peters") announced that the party was intending to form a minority coalition government with the Labour Party of 55 seats, with confidence and supply agreement from the Green Party.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-13) This is the first Government in New Zealand under MMP where the most popular party is not part of the Government. The election resulted in Ardern becoming New Zealand's third female prime minister, and Peters being reappointed [deputy prime minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deputy_Prime_Minister_of_New_Zealand "Deputy Prime Minister of New Zealand"), a role he had first held in 1996–98. This marked an end to nine years under the [Fifth National Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fifth_National_Government_of_New_Zealand "Fifth National Government of New Zealand"), and the beginning of the [Sixth Labour Government of New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixth_Labour_Government_of_New_Zealand "Sixth Labour Government of New Zealand").

## Electoral system

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2017_New_Zealand_general_election&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Electoral system")]

Main article: [Electoral system of New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_system_of_New_Zealand "Electoral system of New Zealand")

New Zealand uses the [mixed-member proportional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed-member_proportional "Mixed-member proportional") (MMP) voting system to elect the 120-member House of Representatives. Each voter gets two votes, one for a political party (the party vote) and one for a local candidate (the electorate vote). Political parties which meet the [threshold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_threshold "Electoral threshold") (5% of the party vote or one electorate seat) receive seats in the House in proportion to the percentage of the party vote they receive. In the 2014 and 2017 elections, 71 of the 120 seats were filled by the MPs elected from the [electorates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_electorates "New Zealand electorates"), with the winner in each electorate determined by the [plurality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plurality_vote "Plurality vote") ("[first-past-the-post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First-past-the-post "First-past-the-post")") method; the remaining 49 seats were filled by candidates from each party's closed [party list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Party_list "Party list"). If a party wins more electorates than seats it is entitled to under the party vote, an [overhang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overhang_seat "Overhang seat") results; in this case, the House will add extra seats to cover the overhang. The 2014 election saw a one-seat overhang where [Peter Dunne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Dunne "Peter Dunne") won the [Ōhāriu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C5%8Ch%C4%81riu "Ōhāriu") electorate when his [United Future Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Future_New_Zealand "United Future New Zealand") was entitled to zero seats under the party vote.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-14)

The majority of members in the House will form a [Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Government "New Zealand Government"). Since it is difficult for any single party to win a [majority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Majority_government "Majority government") of seats under MMP, parties must generally negotiate with other parties either to form a majority [coalition government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coalition_government "Coalition government") or to obtain sufficient [confidence and supply](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confidence_and_supply "Confidence and supply") to operate as a [minority government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minority_government "Minority government").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-15)

Electorate boundaries in the 2017 election were the same as at the 2014 election, with 64 general electorates (48 in the [North Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Island "North Island") and 16 in the [South Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Island "South Island")), and 7 Māori electorates.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### Electoral law changes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2017_New_Zealand_general_election&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Electoral law changes")]

The Electoral Amendment Act 2017 and the Broadcasting (Election Programmes and Election Advertising) Amendment Act 2017 made a number of changes to the conduct of general elections, including:[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-17)

*   Voters no longer have to complete and sign a new enrolment form if they are already enrolled and notify of a change of address, for example, through [New Zealand Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Post "New Zealand Post")'s mail redirection service.
*   The Electoral Commission no longer is required to send out nominations and polling place information to every voter by post; instead the Commission may use its discretion on how to advertise nominations and polling places.
*   Polling booths may now use electronic electoral rolls to mark off voters.
*   Counting of advance votes may now start earlier at 9:00 am (previously 2:00 pm), to take into account the increase in people voting in advance.
*   The contact information of sitting MPs, such as business cards and signage on out-of-Parliament offices, has been clarified as not constituting election advertising.
*   Election advertising is now legally prohibited in or near advance polling booths.
*   Election hoardings may now be erected nine weeks before the election (previously two months), so the first day always falls on a Saturday.
*   Parties are no longer allocated free airtime on [Radio New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_New_Zealand "Radio New Zealand") and [Television New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_New_Zealand "Television New Zealand") to broadcast opening and closing addresses.

### Eligibility to vote

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2017_New_Zealand_general_election&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Eligibility to vote")]

To vote in the general election, one must:

*   be on the [electoral roll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_roll "Electoral roll")
*   be aged 18 or over on election day (i.e. born on or before 23 September 1999)
*   be a [New Zealand citizen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_citizen "New Zealand citizen"), [permanent resident](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_permanent_residency "New Zealand permanent residency"), residence visa holder, an Australian citizen or other person entitled to reside in New Zealand indefinitely.
*   have lived in New Zealand for one year or more continuously at some point
*   have been in New Zealand within the last 3 years (for New Zealand citizens) or 1 year (non-New Zealand citizens); public servants and [Defence Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Defence_Force "New Zealand Defence Force") personnel on duty outside New Zealand, including their partners and children, are not subject to this rule.
*   not be expressly disqualified from enrolling or voting (e.g., serving a sentence of imprisonment; convicted of a corrupt election practice).[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-18)

## Election schedule

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2017_New_Zealand_general_election&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Election schedule")]

Unless an early election is called or the election date is set to circumvent holding a by-election, a general election is held every three years. The previous election was held on Saturday, 20 September 2014.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-19)

The [Governor-General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor-General_of_New_Zealand "Governor-General of New Zealand") must issue [writs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Writ_of_election "Writ of election") for an election within seven days of the expiration or dissolution of the [current Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/51st_New_Zealand_Parliament "51st New Zealand Parliament").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-20) Under section 17 of the [Constitution Act 1986](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_Act_1986 "Constitution Act 1986"), Parliament expires three years "from the day fixed for the return of the writs issued for the last preceding general election of members of the House of Representatives, and no longer." The writs for the 2014 election were returned on 10 October 2014, a day late due to a judicial recount of the Te Tai Tokerau electorate.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-2014_key_dates-21) As a result, the 51st Parliament would have expired, if not dissolved earlier, on Tuesday, 10 October 2017. Consequently, the last day for issuance of writs of election would have been 17 October 2017. The writs must be returned within 50 days of their issuance (save for any judicial recount or death of a candidate), which would have been Wednesday, 6 December 2017.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-sec139-22) Because polling day must be a Saturday[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-sec139-22) and two weeks is generally required for the counting of special votes, the last possible date for the 2017 general election would have been Saturday, 18 November 2017.

On 1 February 2017, Prime Minister [Bill English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_English "Bill English") announced that the election would be held on Saturday 23 September 2017.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-23) This was the first election since [1975](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1975_New_Zealand_general_election "1975 New Zealand general election") that both major parties, Labour and National, contested under new leadership.

Key dates relating to the general election were as follows.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-24)

1 February 2017 (Wednesday)Prime Minister Bill English announces election to be held on 23 September.
23 June 2017 (Friday)The regulated election advertising period begins.
22 July 2017 (Saturday)Election hoardings may be erected (subject to local council rules).
17 August 2017 (Wednesday)Last sitting day for the 51st Parliament.
22 August 2017 (Tuesday)The 51st Parliament is dissolved with a short ceremony on the steps of Parliament House.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-25)
23 August 2017 (Wednesday)**Writ day** – Governor-General issues formal direction to the [Electoral Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_Commission_(New_Zealand) "Electoral Commission (New Zealand)") to hold the election.  
Last day to ordinarily enrol to vote (late enrolments must cast special votes).  
 Official campaigning begins; radio and television advertising begins.
28 August 2017 (Monday)Deadline (12:00) for registered parties to lodge bulk nominations of candidates and party lists.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-Party_Secretary_Handbook-26)
29 August 2017 (Tuesday)Deadline (12:00) for individual candidates to lodge nominations.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-Party_Secretary_Handbook-26)
30 August 2017 (Wednesday)Details of candidates for election and polling places released.
6 September 2017 (Wednesday)Overseas voting begins.
11 September 2017 (Monday)Advance voting begins.
22 September 2017 (Friday)Advance voting ends; overseas voting ends at 16:00 local time.   
Last day to enrol to vote.  
The regulated election advertising period ends; all election advertising must be taken down by midnight.
23 September 2017 (Saturday)**Election day** – polling places open 09:00 to 19:00.   
Preliminary results released progressively after 19:00.
7 October 2017 (Saturday)**Official results declared.**
12 October 2017 (Thursday)Writ for election returned; official declaration of elected members (subject to judicial recounts).

## Results

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2017_New_Zealand_general_election&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Results")]

Further information: [Results of the 2017 New Zealand general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Results_of_the_2017_New_Zealand_general_election "Results of the 2017 New Zealand general election")

Preliminary results were gradually released after polling booths closed at 19:00 ([NZST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Standard_Time "New Zealand Standard Time")) on 23 September. The preliminary count only includes advance ordinary and election day ordinary votes; it does not include any [special votes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_vote "Special vote"). Special votes include votes from those who enrolled after the deadline of 23 August, those who voted outside their electorate (this includes all overseas votes), hospital votes, and those voters enrolled on the unpublished roll.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-PreliminaryResults-56)

All voting papers, counterfoils and electoral rolls are returned to the electorate's returning officer for a mandatory recount; this also includes approving and counting any special votes, and compiling a master roll to ensure no voter has voted more than once. Official results, including all recounted ordinary votes and special votes, were released by the [Electoral Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_Commission_(New_Zealand) "Electoral Commission (New Zealand)") on Saturday 7 October 2017.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-OfficialResults-11)

Parties and candidates have three working days after the release of the official results to apply for a [judicial recount](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Election_recount "Election recount"). These recounts take place under the auspices of a [District Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/District_Court_of_New_Zealand "District Court of New Zealand") judge (the Chief District Court Judge in case of a nationwide recount),[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-57) and may delay the return of the election writ by a few days.

### Electorate results

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2017_New_Zealand_general_election&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Electorate results")]

[![Image 87](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9f/New_Zealand_electorates%2C_2017.svg/330px-New_Zealand_electorates%2C_2017.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:New_Zealand_electorates,_2017.svg)

Party affiliation of winning electorate candidates.

Prior to the election, the National Party held the majority of the electorate seats with 40. Labour held 27 seats, and NZ First, ACT, and United Future held one seat each. Between the 2014 and 2017 elections, one seat changed allegiance: in the [2015 Northland by-election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Northland_by-election "2015 Northland by-election"), NZ First leader Winston Peters won the seat off National, after MP [Mike Sabin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Sabin "Mike Sabin") resigned.

Fifty-five electorates saw the incumbent MP re-elected, while another 11 saw a new MP elected from the same party as the retiring incumbent.

In three electorates, the incumbent MP was defeated. Labour candidate and lawyer [Duncan Webb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duncan_Webb "Duncan Webb") claimed [Christchurch Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christchurch_Central_(New_Zealand_electorate) "Christchurch Central (New Zealand electorate)") off National MP [Nicky Wagner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicky_Wagner "Nicky Wagner"); Labour previously held the electorate continuously from its formation in 1946 until Wagner won it in 2011. After National lost [Northland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northland_(New_Zealand_electorate) "Northland (New Zealand electorate)") to NZ First leader Winston Peters in 2015, candidate [Matt King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_King_(politician) "Matt King (politician)") claimed the electorate back for National from Peters. Labour candidate and former television presenter [Tāmati Coffey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C4%81mati_Coffey "Tāmati Coffey") claimed [Waiariki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waiariki_(New_Zealand_electorate) "Waiariki (New Zealand electorate)") off Māori Party MP [Te Ururoa Flavell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Te_Ururoa_Flavell "Te Ururoa Flavell"); Flavell's defeat saw the Māori Party without an electorate seat and with the party polling below 5% in the party vote, saw the party voted out of Parliament. Coffey's win also saw Labour claim a clean sweep of the Māori electorates for the first time since the 2002 election.

In [Hutt South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hutt_South "Hutt South"), National list MP [Chris Bishop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Bishop_(politician) "Chris Bishop (politician)") claimed the electorate from Labour – the first time the electorate has swung since its creation in 1996. Contributing to the swing was the 2014 boundary changes which saw the Labour-leaning suburb of [Naenae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naenae "Naenae") swapped for the National-leaning western hill suburbs of [Lower Hutt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Hutt "Lower Hutt"), and long standing Labour MP [Trevor Mallard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trevor_Mallard "Trevor Mallard") standing down at the election to contest the party list only. In [Ōhāriu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C5%8Ch%C4%81riu "Ōhāriu"), incumbent United Future MP [Peter Dunne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Dunne "Peter Dunne") stepped down after holding the electorate in various incarnations since 1984. Labour candidate and former police officer [Greg O'Connor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greg_O'Connor_(politician) "Greg O'Connor (politician)") subsequently claimed the electorate.

Overall, National gained one electorate to hold 41, Labour gained two electorates to hold 29, while ACT retained its one electorate seat.

[Hamilton West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamilton_West_(New_Zealand_electorate) "Hamilton West (New Zealand electorate)") was considered to be New Zealand's [bellwether](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellwether_(politics) "Bellwether (politics)") seat.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-60)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-61) Since the formation of the electorate in 1969, the winning candidate was from the party that went on to form the government, with the exception of 1993 when it elected a Labour MP while National went on to form the government (albeit with a one-seat majority). Hamilton West, [Maungakiekie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maungakiekie_(New_Zealand_electorate) "Maungakiekie (New Zealand electorate)") and [Rotorua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotorua_(New_Zealand_electorate) "Rotorua (New Zealand electorate)") were also regarded as bellwethers in the MMP era, swinging with the government at every election since 1996. All three electorates in the 2017 election were won by National candidates.

The **2017 New Zealand general election** took place on Saturday 23 September 2017 to determine the membership of the [52nd New Zealand Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/52nd_New_Zealand_Parliament "52nd New Zealand Parliament"). The [previous parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/51st_New_Zealand_Parliament "51st New Zealand Parliament") was elected on 20 September 2014 and was officially dissolved on 22 August 2017.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-1) Voters elected 120 members to the House of Representatives under New Zealand's [mixed-member proportional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed-member_proportional_representation "Mixed-member proportional representation") (MMP) voting system, a [proportional representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proportional_representation "Proportional representation") system in which 71 members were elected from single-member [electorates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_electorates "New Zealand electorates") and 49 members were elected from [closed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed_list "Closed list")[party lists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Party_list "Party list"). Around 3.57 million people were registered to vote in the election,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-2) with 2.63 million (79.8%) turning out.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-3)[Advance voting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_voting "Early voting") proved popular, with 1.24 million votes cast before election day, more than the previous two elections combined.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-5)

Prior to the election, the centre-right [National Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_National_Party "New Zealand National Party"), led by Prime Minister [Bill English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_English "Bill English"), had [governed since 2008](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fifth_National_Government_of_New_Zealand "Fifth National Government of New Zealand") in a [minority government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minority_government "Minority government") with [confidence and supply](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confidence_and_supply "Confidence and supply") from the [Māori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C4%81ori_Party "Māori Party"), [ACT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACT_New_Zealand "ACT New Zealand") and [United Future](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Future "United Future") parties. It was the first election for English as incumbent prime minister, having replaced [John Key](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Key "John Key") on 12 December 2016 and the first since [1975](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1975_New_Zealand_general_election "1975 New Zealand general election") where both major parties had leadership changes. The main opposition parties to the National government were [Labour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party "New Zealand Labour Party") (the [official opposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_Opposition_(New_Zealand) "Official Opposition (New Zealand)")), led by [Jacinda Ardern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacinda_Ardern "Jacinda Ardern"), the [Green Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Party_of_Aotearoa_New_Zealand "Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand"), and [New Zealand First](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_First "New Zealand First").

The National Party won a [plurality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plurality_(voting) "Plurality (voting)") of the seats with 56, down from 60 in 2014.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-6) Labour made large gains following Jacinda Ardern [becoming the party leader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_Labour_Party_leadership_election "2017 New Zealand Labour Party leadership election") seven weeks prior to the election, increasing its representation from 32 to 46 seats. Labour was the only parliamentary party to gain support but a large portion came at the expense of the Green Party, which lost almost half its seats (dropping from 14 to 8) following co-leader [Metiria Turei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metiria_Turei "Metiria Turei")'s resignation over self-admitted prior welfare benefit and electoral fraud. The anti-immigration populist party New Zealand First won 9 seats, down from 12 in 2014. ACT retained its one seat. Election-night counts had National with 58 seats, Labour with 45 seats, and the Greens with 7 seats, but when [special votes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_vote "Special vote") were counted, National lost one list seat each to the Greens and Labour.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-8)

The election saw five parties return to Parliament, down from seven in 2014 and the lowest number since the introduction of MMP in 1996. [Māori Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C4%81ori_Party "Māori Party") co-leader [Te Ururoa Flavell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Te_Ururoa_Flavell "Te Ururoa Flavell") lost his seat of [Waiariki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waiariki_(New_Zealand_electorate) "Waiariki (New Zealand electorate)") and, with the party's vote count being below the [threshold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_threshold "Electoral threshold") of 5%, they also lost their list MP, co-leader [Marama Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marama_Fox "Marama Fox"), and departed Parliament. [United Future](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Future "United Future") leader and sole MP [Peter Dunne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Dunne "Peter Dunne") retired from politics during the campaign due to poor polling in his electorate of [Ōhāriu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C5%8Ch%C4%81riu "Ōhāriu") and his successor failed to win the seat. The party voted to dissolve less than two months later.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-9)

Even with support partner ACT retaining its sole seat, the existing National minority government were short of the 61 seats needed to govern, and Bill English declared that the arrangement would not be continued.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-StuffNZ-negotiations-10) New Zealand First's nine seats gave it the [balance of power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balance_of_power_(parliament) "Balance of power (parliament)") between the National Party and the Labour–Green bloc.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-OfficialResults-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-ABC-FinalTally-12) On 19 October 2017, New Zealand First leader [Winston Peters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winston_Peters "Winston Peters") announced that the party was intending to form a minority coalition government with the Labour Party of 55 seats, with confidence and supply agreement from the Green Party.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-13) This is the first Government in New Zealand under MMP where the most popular party is not part of the Government. The election resulted in Ardern becoming New Zealand's third female prime minister, and Peters being reappointed [deputy prime minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deputy_Prime_Minister_of_New_Zealand "Deputy Prime Minister of New Zealand"), a role he had first held in 1996–98. This marked an end to nine years under the [Fifth National Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fifth_National_Government_of_New_Zealand "Fifth National Government of New Zealand"), and the beginning of the [Sixth Labour Government of New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixth_Labour_Government_of_New_Zealand "Sixth Labour Government of New Zealand").

## Electoral system

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2017_New_Zealand_general_election&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Electoral system")]

Main article: [Electoral system of New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_system_of_New_Zealand "Electoral system of New Zealand")

New Zealand uses the [mixed-member proportional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed-member_proportional "Mixed-member proportional") (MMP) voting system to elect the 120-member House of Representatives. Each voter gets two votes, one for a political party (the party vote) and one for a local candidate (the electorate vote). Political parties which meet the [threshold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_threshold "Electoral threshold") (5% of the party vote or one electorate seat) receive seats in the House in proportion to the percentage of the party vote they receive. In the 2014 and 2017 elections, 71 of the 120 seats were filled by the MPs elected from the [electorates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_electorates "New Zealand electorates"), with the winner in each electorate determined by the [plurality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plurality_vote "Plurality vote") ("[first-past-the-post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First-past-the-post "First-past-the-post")") method; the remaining 49 seats were filled by candidates from each party's closed [party list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Party_list "Party list"). If a party wins more electorates than seats it is entitled to under the party vote, an [overhang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overhang_seat "Overhang seat") results; in this case, the House will add extra seats to cover the overhang. The 2014 election saw a one-seat overhang where [Peter Dunne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Dunne "Peter Dunne") won the [Ōhāriu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C5%8Ch%C4%81riu "Ōhāriu") electorate when his [United Future Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Future_New_Zealand "United Future New Zealand") was entitled to zero seats under the party vote.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-14)

The majority of members in the House will form a [Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Government "New Zealand Government"). Since it is difficult for any single party to win a [majority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Majority_government "Majority government") of seats under MMP, parties must generally negotiate with other parties either to form a majority [coalition government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coalition_government "Coalition government") or to obtain sufficient [confidence and supply](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confidence_and_supply "Confidence and supply") to operate as a [minority government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minority_government "Minority government").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-15)

Electorate boundaries in the 2017 election were the same as at the 2014 election, with 64 general electorates (48 in the [North Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Island "North Island") and 16 in the [South Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Island "South Island")), and 7 Māori electorates.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### Electoral law changes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2017_New_Zealand_general_election&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Electoral law changes")]

The Electoral Amendment Act 2017 and the Broadcasting (Election Programmes and Election Advertising) Amendment Act 2017 made a number of changes to the conduct of general elections, including:[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-17)

*   Voters no longer have to complete and sign a new enrolment form if they are already enrolled and notify of a change of address, for example, through [New Zealand Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Post "New Zealand Post")'s mail redirection service.
*   The Electoral Commission no longer is required to send out nominations and polling place information to every voter by post; instead the Commission may use its discretion on how to advertise nominations and polling places.
*   Polling booths may now use electronic electoral rolls to mark off voters.
*   Counting of advance votes may now start earlier at 9:00 am (previously 2:00 pm), to take into account the increase in people voting in advance.
*   The contact information of sitting MPs, such as business cards and signage on out-of-Parliament offices, has been clarified as not constituting election advertising.
*   Election advertising is now legally prohibited in or near advance polling booths.
*   Election hoardings may now be erected nine weeks before the election (previously two months), so the first day always falls on a Saturday.
*   Parties are no longer allocated free airtime on [Radio New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_New_Zealand "Radio New Zealand") and [Television New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_New_Zealand "Television New Zealand") to broadcast opening and closing addresses.

### Eligibility to vote

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2017_New_Zealand_general_election&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Eligibility to vote")]

To vote in the general election, one must:

*   be on the [electoral roll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_roll "Electoral roll")
*   be aged 18 or over on election day (i.e. born on or before 23 September 1999)
*   be a [New Zealand citizen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_citizen "New Zealand citizen"), [permanent resident](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_permanent_residency "New Zealand permanent residency"), residence visa holder, an Australian citizen or other person entitled to reside in New Zealand indefinitely.
*   have lived in New Zealand for one year or more continuously at some point
*   have been in New Zealand within the last 3 years (for New Zealand citizens) or 1 year (non-New Zealand citizens); public servants and [Defence Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Defence_Force "New Zealand Defence Force") personnel on duty outside New Zealand, including their partners and children, are not subject to this rule.
*   not be expressly disqualified from enrolling or voting (e.g., serving a sentence of imprisonment; convicted of a corrupt election practice).[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-18)

## Election schedule

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2017_New_Zealand_general_election&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Election schedule")]

Unless an early election is called or the election date is set to circumvent holding a by-election, a general election is held every three years. The previous election was held on Saturday, 20 September 2014.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-19)

The [Governor-General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor-General_of_New_Zealand "Governor-General of New Zealand") must issue [writs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Writ_of_election "Writ of election") for an election within seven days of the expiration or dissolution of the [current Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/51st_New_Zealand_Parliament "51st New Zealand Parliament").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-20) Under section 17 of the [Constitution Act 1986](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_Act_1986 "Constitution Act 1986"), Parliament expires three years "from the day fixed for the return of the writs issued for the last preceding general election of members of the House of Representatives, and no longer." The writs for the 2014 election were returned on 10 October 2014, a day late due to a judicial recount of the Te Tai Tokerau electorate.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-2014_key_dates-21) As a result, the 51st Parliament would have expired, if not dissolved earlier, on Tuesday, 10 October 2017. Consequently, the last day for issuance of writs of election would have been 17 October 2017. The writs must be returned within 50 days of their issuance (save for any judicial recount or death of a candidate), which would have been Wednesday, 6 December 2017.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-sec139-22) Because polling day must be a Saturday[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-sec139-22) and two weeks is generally required for the counting of special votes, the last possible date for the 2017 general election would have been Saturday, 18 November 2017.

On 1 February 2017, Prime Minister [Bill English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_English "Bill English") announced that the election would be held on Saturday 23 September 2017.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-23) This was the first election since [1975](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1975_New_Zealand_general_election "1975 New Zealand general election") that both major parties, Labour and National, contested under new leadership.

Key dates relating to the general election were as follows.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-24)

1 February 2017 (Wednesday)Prime Minister Bill English announces election to be held on 23 September.
23 June 2017 (Friday)The regulated election advertising period begins.
22 July 2017 (Saturday)Election hoardings may be erected (subject to local council rules).

Last day to ordinarily enrol to vote (late enrolments must cast special votes).  
 Official campaigning begins; radio and television advertising begins.
28 August 2017 (Monday)Deadline (12:00) for registered parties to lodge bulk nominations of candidates and party lists.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-Party_Secretary_Handbook-26)
29 August 2017 (Tuesday)Deadline (12:00) for individual candidates to lodge nominations.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-Party_Secretary_Handbook-26)

6 September 2017 (Wednesday)Overseas voting begins.

22 September 2017 (Friday)Advance voting ends; overseas voting ends at 16:00 local time.

## Results

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2017_New_Zealand_general_election&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Results")]

Further information: [Results of the 2017 New Zealand general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Results_of_the_2017_New_Zealand_general_election "Results of the 2017 New Zealand general election")

Preliminary results were gradually released after polling booths closed at 19:00 ([NZST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Standard_Time "New Zealand Standard Time")) on 23 September. The preliminary count only includes advance ordinary and election day ordinary votes; it does not include any [special votes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_vote "Special vote"). Special votes include votes from those who enrolled after the deadline of 23 August, those who voted outside their electorate (this includes all overseas votes), hospital votes, and those voters enrolled on the unpublished roll.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-PreliminaryResults-56)

All voting papers, counterfoils and electoral rolls are returned to the electorate's returning officer for a mandatory recount; this also includes approving and counting any special votes, and compiling a master roll to ensure no voter has voted more than once. Official results, including all recounted ordinary votes and special votes, were released by the [Electoral Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_Commission_(New_Zealand) "Electoral Commission (New Zealand)") on Saturday 7 October 2017.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-OfficialResults-11)

Parties and candidates have three working days after the release of the official results to apply for a [judicial recount](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Election_recount "Election recount"). These recounts take place under the auspices of a [District Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/District_Court_of_New_Zealand "District Court of New Zealand") judge (the Chief District Court Judge in case of a nationwide recount),[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-57) and may delay the return of the election writ by a few days.

### Electorate results

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2017_New_Zealand_general_election&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Electorate results")]

[![Image 87](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9f/New_Zealand_electorates%2C_2017.svg/330px-New_Zealand_electorates%2C_2017.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:New_Zealand_electorates,_2017.svg)

Party affiliation of winning electorate candidates.

Prior to the election, the National Party held the majority of the electorate seats with 40. Labour held 27 seats, and NZ First, ACT, and United Future held one seat each. Between the 2014 and 2017 elections, one seat changed allegiance: in the [2015 Northland by-election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Northland_by-election "2015 Northland by-election"), NZ First leader Winston Peters won the seat off National, after MP [Mike Sabin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Sabin "Mike Sabin") resigned.

Fifty-five electorates saw the incumbent MP re-elected, while another 11 saw a new MP elected from the same party as the retiring incumbent.

In three electorates, the incumbent MP was defeated. Labour candidate and lawyer [Duncan Webb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duncan_Webb "Duncan Webb") claimed [Christchurch Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christchurch_Central_(New_Zealand_electorate) "Christchurch Central (New Zealand electorate)") off National MP [Nicky Wagner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicky_Wagner "Nicky Wagner"); Labour previously held the electorate continuously from its formation in 1946 until Wagner won it in 2011. After National lost [Northland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northland_(New_Zealand_electorate) "Northland (New Zealand electorate)") to NZ First leader Winston Peters in 2015, candidate [Matt King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_King_(politician) "Matt King (politician)") claimed the electorate back for National from Peters. Labour candidate and former television presenter [Tāmati Coffey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C4%81mati_Coffey "Tāmati Coffey") claimed [Waiariki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waiariki_(New_Zealand_electorate) "Waiariki (New Zealand electorate)") off Māori Party MP [Te Ururoa Flavell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Te_Ururoa_Flavell "Te Ururoa Flavell"); Flavell's defeat saw the Māori Party without an electorate seat and with the party polling below 5% in the party vote, saw the party voted out of Parliament. Coffey's win also saw Labour claim a clean sweep of the Māori electorates for the first time since the 2002 election.

In [Hutt South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hutt_South "Hutt South"), National list MP [Chris Bishop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Bishop_(politician) "Chris Bishop (politician)") claimed the electorate from Labour – the first time the electorate has swung since its creation in 1996. Contributing to the swing was the 2014 boundary changes which saw the Labour-leaning suburb of [Naenae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naenae "Naenae") swapped for the National-leaning western hill suburbs of [Lower Hutt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Hutt "Lower Hutt"), and long standing Labour MP [Trevor Mallard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trevor_Mallard "Trevor Mallard") standing down at the election to contest the party list only. In [Ōhāriu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C5%8Ch%C4%81riu "Ōhāriu"), incumbent United Future MP [Peter Dunne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Dunne "Peter Dunne") stepped down after holding the electorate in various incarnations since 1984. Labour candidate and former police officer [Greg O'Connor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greg_O'Connor_(politician) "Greg O'Connor (politician)") subsequently claimed the electorate.

Overall, National gained one electorate to hold 41, Labour gained two electorates to hold 29, while ACT retained its one electorate seat.

[Hamilton West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamilton_West_(New_Zealand_electorate) "Hamilton West (New Zealand electorate)") was considered to be New Zealand's [bellwether](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellwether_(politics) "Bellwether (politics)") seat.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-60)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_Zealand_general_election#cite_note-61) Since the formation of the electorate in 1969, the winning candidate was from the party that went on to form the government, with the exception of 1993 when it elected a Labour MP while National went on to form the government (albeit with a one-seat majority). Hamilton West, [Maungakiekie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maungakiekie_(New_Zealand_electorate) "Maungakiekie (New Zealand electorate)") and [Rotorua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotorua_(New_Zealand_electorate) "Rotorua (New Zealand electorate)") were also regarded as bellwethers in the MMP era, swinging with the government at every election since 1996. All three electorates in the 2017 election were won by National candidates.

The **54th New Zealand Parliament** is the current meeting of the legislature in [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand "New Zealand"). It opened on 5 December 2023 following the [14 October 2023 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_New_Zealand_general_election "2023 New Zealand general election"), and will expire on or before 16 November 2026 to trigger the [2026 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_New_Zealand_general_election "2026 New Zealand general election").

The Parliament was elected using a [mixed-member proportional representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed-member_proportional_representation "Mixed-member proportional representation") (MMP) voting system. MPs represent 72 [geographical electorates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_electorates "New Zealand electorates"): 16 in the [South Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Island "South Island"), 49 in the [North Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Island "North Island") and 7 [Māori electorates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C4%81ori_electorates "Māori electorates"). The [Electoral Act 1993](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_Act_1993 "Electoral Act 1993") provides for the remaining seats to be elected from [party lists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Party_lists_in_the_2023_New_Zealand_general_election "Party lists in the 2023 New Zealand general election") using the [Sainte-Laguë method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sainte-Lagu%C3%AB_method "Sainte-Laguë method") to realise proportionality to an expected total of at least 120 MPs.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-1)

Final results of the election determined that there are 123 members of Parliament, rather than the usual 120. 122 members were elected in the general election (there is an [overhang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overhang_seat "Overhang seat") of two members for [Te Pāti Māori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Te_P%C4%81ti_M%C4%81ori "Te Pāti Māori")).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-3) Due to the death of a candidate between the close of nominations and election day, [Port Waikato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Waikato_(New_Zealand_electorate) "Port Waikato (New Zealand electorate)") did not elect a representative and an additional list MP was elected to ensure Parliament would have at least 120 members. The 72nd electorate MP, and 123rd MP overall, was elected in the [Port Waikato by-election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Port_Waikato_by-election "2023 Port Waikato by-election") on 25 November 2023.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-NZH_9_Oct-4) In May 2026 following Judith Collins appointment to President of the New Zealand Law Commission, she resigned her electorate seat which lowered the number of MPs to 122.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-5)

Members in the 54th Parliament represent six [political parties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_political_parties_in_New_Zealand "List of political parties in New Zealand"): [National](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_National_Party "New Zealand National Party"), [ACT New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACT_New_Zealand "ACT New Zealand"), [New Zealand First](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_First "New Zealand First") parties, in [government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_(government) "Executive (government)"), and the [Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party "New Zealand Labour Party"), [Green Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Party_of_Aotearoa_New_Zealand "Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand"), and Te Pāti Māori, in [opposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_opposition "Parliamentary opposition"). [Christopher Luxon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Luxon "Christopher Luxon") of the National Party formed a coalition government with ACT and New Zealand First and was sworn in as prime minister on 27 November 2023.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-1news.co.nz-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-TVNZ-7)

### 2023 general election

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=54th_New_Zealand_Parliament&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 2023 general election")]

Main article: [2023 New Zealand general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_New_Zealand_general_election "2023 New Zealand general election")

The 2023 general election was held on 14 October. The opposition [National Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_National_Party "New Zealand National Party") won 48 seats in the election, an increase of 14 seats. The ruling [Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party "New Zealand Labour Party") was reduced to 34 seats after losing a total of 28 seats. The [Green Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Party_of_Aotearoa_New_Zealand "Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand"), Labour's cooperation partner, got 15 seats, a rise of 6. The [ACT Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACT_New_Zealand "ACT New Zealand") increased its seat count by one. [Te Pāti Māori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Te_P%C4%81ti_M%C4%81ori "Te Pāti Māori") took five Maori seats from Labour, totaling six seats, one more than their party vote entitled them to, giving parliament a three-seat overhang. After being voted out in the [2020 New Zealand general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_New_Zealand_general_election "2020 New Zealand general election"), [New Zealand First](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_First "New Zealand First") returned to parliament, earning eight seats.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-8)

### Government formation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=54th_New_Zealand_Parliament&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Government formation")]

Main article: [Sixth National Government of New Zealand §Coalition negotiations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixth_National_Government_of_New_Zealand#Coalition_negotiations "Sixth National Government of New Zealand")

Following the general election, the National Party required support from the ACT Party and New Zealand First to command the confidence of the House.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-9) Negotiations between the three parties took place after the official results were announced on 3 November. After three weeks of negotiations, [Christopher Luxon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Luxon "Christopher Luxon") announced the formation of a coalition government with ACT and New Zealand First on 24 November.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-1news.co.nz-6) On 27 November, Luxon was sworn in as prime minister by Governor-General [Dame Cindy Kiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dame_Cindy_Kiro "Dame Cindy Kiro").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-TVNZ-7)

## Parliamentary term

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=54th_New_Zealand_Parliament&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Parliamentary term")]

The final results of the election were announced on 3 November and the writ for the 2023 election was returned on 16 November 2023.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-11) Under section 19 of Constitution Act 1986, Parliament must meet no later than six weeks after this date; on 29 November 2023, following the new government's first Cabinet meeting, Leader of the House [Chris Bishop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Bishop "Chris Bishop") confirmed that the Commission Opening and State Opening of Parliament would take place on 5 and 6 December 2023, respectively.

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=54th_New_Zealand_Parliament&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Timeline")]

*   16 November 2023 – The writ for election is returned; officially declaring all elected members of the 54th Parliament.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-12)
*   24 November 2023 – A coalition government is formed between [National](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_National_Party "New Zealand National Party"), [ACT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACT_New_Zealand "ACT New Zealand"), and [NZ First](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_First "New Zealand First").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-1news.co.nz-6)
*   27 November 2023 – [Christopher Luxon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Luxon "Christopher Luxon") is sworn in as [Prime Minister of New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_New_Zealand "Prime Minister of New Zealand").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-TVNZ-7)
*   5 December 2023 – The Governor-General issued the Commission of Opening of Parliament. The House elects [Gerry Brownlee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerry_Brownlee "Gerry Brownlee") as [Speaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speaker_of_the_New_Zealand_House_of_Representatives "Speaker of the New Zealand House of Representatives").

*   17–21 June 2024 – Parliament holds its first ever "scrutiny week," which allows select committees to scrutinise government and public sector spending plans.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-Scrutiny_weeks-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-15)
*   2–6 December 2024 – Parliament is scheduled to hold its second scrutiny week.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-Scrutiny_weeks-14)
*   22 May 2025 – [Budget 2025](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_New_Zealand_budget "2025 New Zealand budget") is delivered to Parliament.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-16)
*   16–20 June 2025 – Scrutiny week.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-17)

*   1–5 December 2025 – Scrutiny week[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-19)
*   15–19 June 2026 – Scrutiny week.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-20)
