The **54th New Zealand Parliament** is the current meeting of the legislature in [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand "New Zealand"). It opened on 5 December 2023 following the [14 October 2023 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_New_Zealand_general_election "2023 New Zealand general election"), and will expire on or before 16 November 2026 to trigger the [2026 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_New_Zealand_general_election "2026 New Zealand general election").

The Parliament was elected using a [mixed-member proportional representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed-member_proportional_representation "Mixed-member proportional representation") (MMP) voting system. MPs represent 72 [geographical electorates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_electorates "New Zealand electorates"): 16 in the [South Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Island "South Island"), 49 in the [North Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Island "North Island") and 7 [Māori electorates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C4%81ori_electorates "Māori electorates"). The [Electoral Act 1993](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_Act_1993 "Electoral Act 1993") provides for the remaining seats to be elected from [party lists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Party_lists_in_the_2023_New_Zealand_general_election "Party lists in the 2023 New Zealand general election") using the [Sainte-Laguë method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sainte-Lagu%C3%AB_method "Sainte-Laguë method") to realise proportionality to an expected total of at least 120 MPs.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-1)

Final results of the election determined that there are 123 members of Parliament, rather than the usual 120. 122 members were elected in the general election (there is an [overhang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overhang_seat "Overhang seat") of two members for [Te Pāti Māori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Te_P%C4%81ti_M%C4%81ori "Te Pāti Māori")).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-3) Due to the death of a candidate between the close of nominations and election day, [Port Waikato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Waikato_(New_Zealand_electorate) "Port Waikato (New Zealand electorate)") did not elect a representative and an additional list MP was elected to ensure Parliament would have at least 120 members. The 72nd electorate MP, and 123rd MP overall, was elected in the [Port Waikato by-election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Port_Waikato_by-election "2023 Port Waikato by-election") on 25 November 2023.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-NZH_9_Oct-4) In May 2026 following Judith Collins appointment to President of the New Zealand Law Commission, she resigned her electorate seat which lowered the number of MPs to 122.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-5)

Members in the 54th Parliament represent six [political parties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_political_parties_in_New_Zealand "List of political parties in New Zealand"): [National](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_National_Party "New Zealand National Party"), [ACT New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACT_New_Zealand "ACT New Zealand"), [New Zealand First](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_First "New Zealand First") parties, in [government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_(government) "Executive (government)"), and the [Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party "New Zealand Labour Party"), [Green Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Party_of_Aotearoa_New_Zealand "Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand"), and Te Pāti Māori, in [opposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_opposition "Parliamentary opposition"). [Christopher Luxon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Luxon "Christopher Luxon") of the National Party formed a coalition government with ACT and New Zealand First and was sworn in as prime minister on 27 November 2023.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-1news.co.nz-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-TVNZ-7)

## Background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=54th_New_Zealand_Parliament&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

### 2023 general election

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=54th_New_Zealand_Parliament&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 2023 general election")]

Main article: [2023 New Zealand general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_New_Zealand_general_election "2023 New Zealand general election")

The 2023 general election was held on 14 October. The opposition [National Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_National_Party "New Zealand National Party") won 48 seats in the election, an increase of 14 seats. The ruling [Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party "New Zealand Labour Party") was reduced to 34 seats after losing a total of 28 seats. The [Green Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Party_of_Aotearoa_New_Zealand "Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand"), Labour's cooperation partner, got 15 seats, a rise of 6. The [ACT Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACT_New_Zealand "ACT New Zealand") increased its seat count by one. [Te Pāti Māori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Te_P%C4%81ti_M%C4%81ori "Te Pāti Māori") took five Maori seats from Labour, totaling six seats, one more than their party vote entitled them to, giving parliament a three-seat overhang. After being voted out in the [2020 New Zealand general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_New_Zealand_general_election "2020 New Zealand general election"), [New Zealand First](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_First "New Zealand First") returned to parliament, earning eight seats.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-8)

### Government formation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=54th_New_Zealand_Parliament&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Government formation")]

Main article: [Sixth National Government of New Zealand §Coalition negotiations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixth_National_Government_of_New_Zealand#Coalition_negotiations "Sixth National Government of New Zealand")

Following the general election, the National Party required support from the ACT Party and New Zealand First to command the confidence of the House.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-9) Negotiations between the three parties took place after the official results were announced on 3 November. After three weeks of negotiations, [Christopher Luxon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Luxon "Christopher Luxon") announced the formation of a coalition government with ACT and New Zealand First on 24 November.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-1news.co.nz-6) On 27 November, Luxon was sworn in as prime minister by Governor-General [Dame Cindy Kiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dame_Cindy_Kiro "Dame Cindy Kiro").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-TVNZ-7)

## Parliamentary term

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=54th_New_Zealand_Parliament&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Parliamentary term")]

The final results of the election were announced on 3 November and the writ for the 2023 election was returned on 16 November 2023.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-11) Under section 19 of Constitution Act 1986, Parliament must meet no later than six weeks after this date; on 29 November 2023, following the new government's first Cabinet meeting, Leader of the House [Chris Bishop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Bishop "Chris Bishop") confirmed that the Commission Opening and State Opening of Parliament would take place on 5 and 6 December 2023, respectively.

### Timeline

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=54th_New_Zealand_Parliament&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Timeline")]

*   16 November 2023 – The writ for election is returned; officially declaring all elected members of the 54th Parliament.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-12)
*   24 November 2023 – A coalition government is formed between [National](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_National_Party "New Zealand National Party"), [ACT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACT_New_Zealand "ACT New Zealand"), and [NZ First](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_First "New Zealand First").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-1news.co.nz-6)
*   27 November 2023 – [Christopher Luxon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Luxon "Christopher Luxon") is sworn in as [Prime Minister of New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_New_Zealand "Prime Minister of New Zealand").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-TVNZ-7)
*   5 December 2023 – The Governor-General issued the Commission of Opening of Parliament. The House elects [Gerry Brownlee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerry_Brownlee "Gerry Brownlee") as [Speaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speaker_of_the_New_Zealand_House_of_Representatives "Speaker of the New Zealand House of Representatives").
*   6 December 2023 – State Opening of Parliament
*   30 May 2024 – [Budget 2024](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_New_Zealand_budget "2024 New Zealand budget") is delivered to Parliament.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-13)
*   17–21 June 2024 – Parliament holds its first ever "scrutiny week," which allows select committees to scrutinise government and public sector spending plans.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-Scrutiny_weeks-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-15)
*   2–6 December 2024 – Parliament is scheduled to hold its second scrutiny week.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-Scrutiny_weeks-14)
*   22 May 2025 – [Budget 2025](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_New_Zealand_budget "2025 New Zealand budget") is delivered to Parliament.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-16)
*   16–20 June 2025 – Scrutiny week.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-17)
*   26 June–15 July 2025 – Parliament adjourns for two weeks following the death of [Takutai Tarsh Kemp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takutai_Tarsh_Kemp "Takutai Tarsh Kemp"), the [Te Pāti Māori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Te_P%C4%81ti_M%C4%81ori "Te Pāti Māori") Member of Parliament for [Tāmaki Makaurau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C4%81maki_Makaurau_(New_Zealand_electorate) "Tāmaki Makaurau (New Zealand electorate)").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-18)
*   1–5 December 2025 – Scrutiny week[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-19)
*   15–19 June 2026 – Scrutiny week.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-20)
*   1 October 2026 – The 54th Parliament is expected to be dissolved, leading up to the [2026 New Zealand general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_New_Zealand_general_election "2026 New Zealand general election") scheduled for 7 November 2026.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-21)

### Major legislation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=54th_New_Zealand_Parliament&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Major legislation")]

See also: [List of acts of the 54th New Zealand Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_acts_of_the_54th_New_Zealand_Parliament "List of acts of the 54th New Zealand Parliament")

#### 2023–2024

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=54th_New_Zealand_Parliament&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 2023–2024")]

In December 2023, the Government repealed several of the previous [Labour Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixth_Labour_Government_of_New_Zealand "Sixth Labour Government of New Zealand")'s legislation and policies including the [Reserve Bank of New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reserve_Bank_of_New_Zealand "Reserve Bank of New Zealand")'s dual mandate, the [Fair Pay Agreements Act 2022](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fair_Pay_Agreements_Act_2022 "Fair Pay Agreements Act 2022"), the [Clean Car Discount](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Transport_(New_Zealand)#Clean_Car_Discount "Ministry of Transport (New Zealand)") programme, the [Natural and Built Environment Act 2023](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_and_Built_Environment_Act_2023 "Natural and Built Environment Act 2023") and the [Spatial Planning Act 2023](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spatial_Planning_Act_2023 "Spatial Planning Act 2023").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-25) On 21 December, the Government passed legislation reinstating 90-day work trials.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-26) In February 2024, the Government repealed the [Three Waters reform programme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Waters_reform_programme "Three Waters reform programme"), [Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act 2022](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smokefree_Environments_and_Regulated_Products_(Smoked_Tobacco)_Amendment_Act_2022 "Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act 2022") and disestablished [Te Aka Whai Ora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Te_Aka_Whai_Ora "Te Aka Whai Ora") (the Māori Health Authority) under urgency.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-29)

In late March 2024, the Government passed major tax legislation restoring interest deductibility for residential investment property, reducing the bright-line test for residential property to two years, and eliminating depreciation deductions for commercial and industrial buildings.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-30) The Government also passed legislation requiring [electric cars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_car "Electric car") and [plug-in hybrids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plug-in_hybrid "Plug-in hybrid") to pay road user charges.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-31) In April 2024, the Government passed the [legislation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Misuse_of_Drugs_(Pseudoephedrine)_Amendment_Act_2024 "Misuse of Drugs (Pseudoephedrine) Amendment Act 2024") allowing 11 [pseudoephedrine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudoephedrine "Pseudoephedrine") cold and flu medicines to be sold without prescriptions from June 2024.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-32)

In late July 2024, the Government passed [legislation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_Government_(Electoral_Legislation_and_M%C4%81ori_Wards_and_M%C4%81ori_Constituencies)_Amendment_Act_2024 "Local Government (Electoral Legislation and Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Act 2024") reinstating the referendum requirement for [Māori wards and constituencies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C4%81ori_wards_and_constituencies "Māori wards and constituencies") in local councils. Councils that had previously established a Māori ward without a referendum are now required to hold a binding poll alongside the [2025 New Zealand local elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_New_Zealand_local_elections "2025 New Zealand local elections") or to disestablish them.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-RNZ_30_Jul_2024-33) In late August 2024, the Government passed [legislation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_Water_Done_Well#Local_Government_(Water_Services_Preliminary_Arrangements)_Act_2024 "Local Water Done Well") requiring local councils to develop plans for delivering drinking water, wastewater and stormwater services as part of its "[Local Water Done Well](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_Water_Done_Well "Local Water Done Well")" programme.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-34)

In September 2024, Parliament passed a private member's bill amending the [Fair Trading Act 1986](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fair_Trading_Act_1986 "Fair Trading Act 1986") to ensure that gift cards have a minimum expiry date of three years from their initial purchase. The bill was supported by all parties except [ACT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACT_New_Zealand "ACT New Zealand").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-35) In mid October 2024, Parliament passed [Deborah Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deborah_Russell "Deborah Russell")'s private member's bill exempting victims of domestic violence from waiting a mandatory two years to seek a divorce.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-36) In late October 2024, National-led government passed the legislation easing the "regulatory burden" on the country's farming, mining and other primary industries.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-37) In late November 2024, Parliament with cross-party support passed [legislation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citizenship_(Western_Samoa)_(Restoration)_Amendment_Act_2024 "Citizenship (Western Samoa) (Restoration) Amendment Act 2024") restoring [New Zealand citizenship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_nationality_law "New Zealand nationality law") to people born in [Samoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samoa "Samoa") between 1924 and 1949, who had been deprived of New Zealand citizenship in 1982.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-38)

On 10 December 2024, Parliament passed urgent legislation banning [greyhound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greyhound "Greyhound") dogs from being killed while the Government took action to end [greyhound racing in New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greyhound_racing_in_New_Zealand "Greyhound racing in New Zealand") by July 2026.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-39) On 12 December, Parliament passed the government's legislation introducing its pet bonds for tenants and reinstating 90 day no-cause evictions.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-40) On 13 December, Parliament passed the government's [legislation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentencing_(Reinstating_Three_Strikes)_Amendment_Act_2024 "Sentencing (Reinstating Three Strikes) Amendment Act 2024") reinstating [three-strikes laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-strikes_law "Three-strikes law").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-NZH_13_Dec_2024-41) On 17 December, the Government's contentious [Fast-track Approvals Act 2024](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fast-track_Approvals_Act_2024 "Fast-track Approvals Act 2024") passed into law.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-42)

#### 2025

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=54th_New_Zealand_Parliament&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 2025")]

On 30 January 2025, Parliament passed the Taranaki Maunga Collective Redress Bill, which conferred legal personhood on [Mount Taranaki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Taranaki "Mount Taranaki"). The [New Zealand Crown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Crown "New Zealand Crown") also apologised to eight Māori [iwi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iwi "Iwi") for confiscating Mount Taranaki and 1.2 million acres of Māori lands in the [Taranaki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taranaki "Taranaki") region. In addition, Mount Egmont would cease to be an official name for Mt Taranaki.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-43)

On 12 March, Parliament passed Labour MP [Camilla Belich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camilla_Belich "Camilla Belich")'s Crimes (Theft By Employer) Amendment Bill, clarifying that an employer withholding an employee's wages is theft. While the bill was opposed by National and ACT (60 votes), it passed with the support of the Labour, Green, Māori and New Zealand First parties (63 votes). The bill received royal assent on 13 March.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-44)

On 7 May, Parliament passed the [Equal Pay Amendment Act 2025](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equal_Pay_Amendment_Act_2025 "Equal Pay Amendment Act 2025") under urgency, raising the threshold for making pay equity claims. As a result, 33 claims representing thousands of workers have to be dropped and refiled. The bill was supported by the governing coalition but opposed by all opposition parties.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-45) On 15 May, Parliament passed legislation formalising a Treaty of Waitangi settlement with [Ngāti Ranginui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ng%C4%81ti_Ranginui "Ngāti Ranginui"); which included NZ$38 million in financial restitution and returning 15 sites of historical significance to the tribe.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-46)

On 26 June, Parliament passed [legislation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oversight_of_Oranga_Tamariki_System_Legislation_Amendment_Act_2025 "Oversight of Oranga Tamariki System Legislation Amendment Act 2025") designating the [Independent Children's Monitor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_Children's_Monitor "Independent Children's Monitor") as a stand-alone independent [Crown entity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_entity "Crown entity"), disestablishing the [Children and Young People's Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_and_Young_People's_Commission "Children and Young People's Commission") and reinstating the [Children's Commissioner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children's_Commissioner_(New_Zealand) "Children's Commissioner (New Zealand)"); effective 1 August 2025. The bill was supported by all parties except Te Pāti Māori.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-47) On 31 July, Parliament passed [legislation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_Minerals_Amendment_Act_2025 "Crown Minerals Amendment Act 2025") repealing a 2018 law limiting new oil and gas exploration permits off the coast of [Taranaki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taranaki "Taranaki") along party lines.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-48)

On 19 August, the Government passed two laws, the Local Government (Water Services) Bill and the Local Government (Water Services) (Repeals and Amendments) Bill, entrenching its [Local Water Done Well](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_Water_Done_Well "Local Water Done Well") framework.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-49) On 20 August, Parliament passed Labour MP [Camilla Belich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camilla_Belich "Camilla Belich")'s bill banning employers from imposing gag orders on workers talking about their salaries passed into law with the support of the Green, Māori, and National parties. That same day, Labour MP [Tracey McLellan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tracey_McLellan "Tracey McLellan")'s bill extending the range of protections for those giving evidence of sexual assaults or family harm in the [Family Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_Court_of_New_Zealand "Family Court of New Zealand") passed into law with unanimous support.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-50)

On 17 September, Parliament passed urgent legislation preventing convicted abusers from adopting children from other countries.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-51) On 14 October, Parliament passed legislation allowing radio and television stations to broadcast advertisements on [Christmas Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christmas_Day "Christmas Day"), [Good Friday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_Friday "Good Friday"), [Easter Sunday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Easter_Sunday "Easter Sunday") and [Anzac Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anzac_Day "Anzac Day"). The legislation was supported by the National, Labour and ACT parties but was opposed by the Greens, New Zealand First and Te Pāti Māori.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-52) On 22 October, Parliament passed the government's [legislation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_and_Coastal_Area_(Takutai_Moana)_(Customary_Marine_Title)_Amendment_Act_2025 "Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Act 2025") limiting the threshold for Māori [foreshore and seabed claims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_foreshore_and_seabed_controversy "New Zealand foreshore and seabed controversy"). Opposition parties vowed to repeal the legislation if they formed the next government.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-53)

On 5 November, Parliament passed legislation formalizing a Treaty of Waitangi settlement with [Ngāti Pāoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ng%C4%81ti_P%C4%81oa "Ngāti Pāoa"). The settlement includes NZ$23.5 million in financial compensation, recognising 12 "culturally significant" sites, and a formal Crown apology for historical land alienation.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-54) On 13 November, ACT leader and Deputy Prime Minister [David Seymour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Seymour "David Seymour")'s contentious [Regulatory Standards Act 2025](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regulatory_Standards_Act_2025 "Regulatory Standards Act 2025") passed its third reading in Parliament, becoming law.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-55)

On 11 December, Parliament passed two urgent government laws delaying a ban on [farrowing crates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farrowing_crate "Farrowing crate") by ten years and [legislation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fast-track_Approvals_Amendment_Act_2025 "Fast-track Approvals Amendment Act 2025") amending the [Fast-track Approvals Act 2024](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fast-track_Approvals_Act_2024 "Fast-track Approvals Act 2024").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-57) On 17 December, Parliament passed [electoral amendment legislation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_Amendment_Act_2025 "Electoral Amendment Act 2025") reducing the timeframe for voter registration to two weeks before election day, banning prisoners from voting and allowing larger anonymous donations.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-58) That same day, Parliament passed a bill implementing the [Nelson Tenths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Tenths "Nelson Tenths") settlement between the [Te Tau Ihu Māori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Te_Tau_Ihu_M%C4%81ori "Te Tau Ihu Māori") and the New Zealand Crown.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-59)

#### 2026

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=54th_New_Zealand_Parliament&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: 2026")]

On 29 January, Parliament passed legislation formalising the Crown's Treaty settlement with [Ngāti Hāua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ng%C4%81ti_H%C4%81ua "Ngāti Hāua"); which includes NZ$19 million worth of financial redress and the return of 64 culturally-significant sites.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-60) On 17 February, Parliament passed the Government's controversial [Employment Relations Amendment Act 2026](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Employment_Relations_Amendment_Act_2026 "Employment Relations Amendment Act 2026") which tightened the criteria for personal grievances claims, created a "gateway test" for differentiating between employees and contractors, ended payouts for employees dismissed for "serious misconduct," and eliminated a 30-day rule extending automatic collective agreement terms to new employees.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-61) That same week, Parliament passed legislation extending [Anzac Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anzac_Day "Anzac Day") recognition to all servicemen who had served New Zealand in conflicts, peacekeeping operations and other deployments.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-62)

In mid-February 2026, [Minister for Infrastructure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_for_Infrastructure_(New_Zealand) "Minister for Infrastructure (New Zealand)")[Chris Bishop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Bishop "Chris Bishop") released the country's first "National Infrastructure Plan." This plan outlines 16 recommendations and 10 priorities for the next decade. Bishop said that the Government would be seeking cross-party support across Parliament for the plan.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-63) By mid-June 2026, the opposition Labour and Green parties agreed to support the bulk of the National Infrastructure Plan's provisions. The Government agreed to implement 13 of the 16 recommendations and four further actions including reviewing the land transport funding system, introducing legislation requiring government departments and [Crown entities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_entity "Crown entity") to develop long-term investment and asset management plans, requiring infrastructure provides to maintain updated data in the National Infrastructure Network and developing a professional standard for public sector leadership.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-64)

On 1 April 2026, Parliament passed Labour MP [Kieran McAnulty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kieran_McAnulty "Kieran McAnulty")'s member's bill allowing more premises open on [Good Friday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_Friday "Good Friday"), [Anzac Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anzac_Day "Anzac Day") and [Christmas Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christmas_Day "Christmas Day") to sell alcohol under normal license conditions, with the exception of liquors stores and supermarkets.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-65) In early April 2026, Parliament passed legislation reducing the [housing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Housing "Housing") intensification target in Auckland by 32.5 percent from 2 million to 1.4 million homes.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-66) On 2 April, Parliament passed legislation creating the legislative framework for phasing out [greyhound racing in New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greyhound_racing_in_New_Zealand "Greyhound racing in New Zealand") by 1 August 2026 including creating a transitional agency and rehoming the dogs.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-67) On 28 April, Parliament passed the Government's controversial legislation legalising online [casinos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casino "Casino") along party lines.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-68)

On 13 May, Parliament passed legislation entrenching three Treaty settlements with three [Hauraki iwi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hauraki_iwi "Hauraki iwi") (tribes): [Ngāti Hei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ng%C4%81ti_Hei "Ngāti Hei"), [Ngāti Tara Tokanui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ng%C4%81ti_Tara_Tokanui "Ngāti Tara Tokanui") and [Ngāti Rāhiri Tumutumu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ng%C4%81ti_R%C4%81hiri_Tumutumu "Ngāti Rāhiri Tumutumu").[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-69) On 27 May, Parliament passed the Government's legislation disestablishing the [Ministry for the Environment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_for_the_Environment_(New_Zealand) "Ministry for the Environment (New Zealand)") and transferring its statutory functions to the new [Ministry for Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_for_Cities,_Environment,_Regions_and_Transport "Ministry for Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport") (MCERT), effective 1 July.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-70) On 29 May, Parliament passed the Government's legislation under urgency allowing the [Ministry of Social Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Social_Development_(New_Zealand) "Ministry of Social Development (New Zealand)") to use artificial intelligence to make decisions regarding people's welfare benefits.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-71)

On 1 July, Parliament passed the Government's contentious legislation reversing several 2015 workplace safety legislative changes that were passed following the 2010 [Pike River Mine disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pike_River_Mine_disaster "Pike River Mine disaster").[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-72) On 28 July, Parliament passed the [Arms Act 2026](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arms_Act_2026?action=edit&redlink=1 "Arms Act 2026 (page does not exist)"), which replaced the [Arms Act 1983](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arms_Act_1983 "Arms Act 1983") as the regulatory framework for [firearms in New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gun_law_in_New_Zealand "Gun law in New Zealand").[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-73) On 29 July, Parliament passed the Government's Employment Leave Bill replacing the Holiday Act. The new law bases employees' annual and sick leave in direct proportion to their standard work hours.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-74) On 30 July, Parliament passed the [English Language Act 2026](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Language_Act_2026 "English Language Act 2026"), which designated the [English language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language "English language") as one of New Zealand's three official languages.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-75)

On 6 August, Parliament passed the Crimes Amendment Bill, which amended the [Crimes Act 1961](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crimes_Act_1961 "Crimes Act 1961") by creating new offences for assaulting first responders and [coward punching](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sucker_punch "Sucker punch"), raised penalties for [shoplifting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shoplifting "Shoplifting") and [human trafficking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_trafficking "Human trafficking"), and expanded [citizen's arrest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citizen's_arrest "Citizen's arrest") powers.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-76) On 18 August, Parliament unanimously passed legislation entrenching the [Nelson Tenths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Tenths "Nelson Tenths") settlement into law.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-77) That same day, Parliament passed the contentious Climate Change Response (Tort Liability) Amendment Bill, which prevents lawsuits against companies for climate changing-emissions under [tort law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tort_law "Tort law").[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-78)

### Workplace behaviour and disciplinary actions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=54th_New_Zealand_Parliament&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Workplace behaviour and disciplinary actions")]

#### Julie Anne Genter

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=54th_New_Zealand_Parliament&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Julie Anne Genter")]

In early May 2024, [Green Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Party_of_Aotearoa_New_Zealand "Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand") MP [Julie Anne Genter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julie_Anne_Genter "Julie Anne Genter") was referred to Parliament's privileges committee following complaints that she intimidated [National Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_National_Party "New Zealand National Party")'s MP [Matt Doocey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Doocey "Matt Doocey") during a heated parliamentary exchange.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-79) In early August 2024, Genter was found in contempt of Parliament and ordered to apologise.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-80)

#### Tākuta Ferris

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=54th_New_Zealand_Parliament&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Tākuta Ferris")]

In late September 2024, [Te Pati Māori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Te_Pati_M%C4%81ori "Te Pati Māori") MP [Tākuta Ferris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C4%81kuta_Ferris "Tākuta Ferris") was referred to Parliament's Privileges Committee after he made remarks accused Members of Parliament of lying and obfuscation.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-81) On 12 February 2025, the Privileges Committee found that Ferris deliberately misled the House and ordered that he apologise for calling other MPs "liars".[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-82)

#### 2024 Treaty Principles Bill haka

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=54th_New_Zealand_Parliament&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: 2024 Treaty Principles Bill haka")]

On 10 December 2024, Labour MP [Peeni Henare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peeni_Henare "Peeni Henare"), Te Pāti Māori MPs [Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hana-Rawhiti_Maipi-Clarke "Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke"), co-leaders [Rawiri Waititi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rawiri_Waititi "Rawiri Waititi") and [Debbie Ngarewa-Packer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Ngarewa-Packer "Debbie Ngarewa-Packer") were referred to the Privileges Committee for leading a [haka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haka "Haka") (ka mate) that interrupted vote proceedings during the first reading of the [Treaty Principles Bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_Principles_Bill "Treaty Principles Bill") on 14 November.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-83) On 26 March, the Committee found that Henare had acted in a "disorderly" way in joining the Te Pāti Māori-led haka but ruled that his actions did not amount to "contempt."[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-84)

On 1 April 2025, Maipi-Clark, Waititi and Ngarewa-Packer declined to appear before the Privileges Committee, claiming they had been denied key legal rights such as a joint hearing, restrictions on their legal representation [Christopher Finlayson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Finlayson "Christopher Finlayson"), expert testimony from [tikanga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tikanga "Tikanga") (Māori culture) expert Tā Pou Temara denied, hearing scheduling conflicts being ignored and concerns about disciplinary action against Maipi-Clarke.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-85) On 2 April, Chairperson of Privileges Committee [Judith Collins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Collins "Judith Collins") confirmed that the privileges hearing would go ahead regardless of whether the three TPM MPs turned up.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-86) In response, Ngarewa-Packer and Waititi announced that Te Pāti Māori would boycott the hearing and hold its own "alternative independent hearing," dismissing the Privileges Committee as a "[kangaroo court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kangaroo_court "Kangaroo court")."[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-87)

On 14 May, the Privileges Committee censured Maipi-Clark, Ngarewa-Packer and Waititi for "acting in a manner that could have the effect of intimidating a member of the House in the discharge of their duty" during the haka protest. Maipi-Clark was suspended from Parliament for seven days while the two co-leaders were suspended from Parliament for 21 days. The Privileges Committee's chair [Judith Collins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Collins "Judith Collins") declined to confirm whether Parliamentary protocol would be updated to accommodate more [Tikanga Māori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tikanga_M%C4%81ori "Tikanga Māori"). Te Pāti Māori issued a statement denouncing the verdict as punishment by colonial powers meant to intimidate them.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-88)

On 20 May, Parliament held a debate on the Privileges Committee's recommendation to suspend three Te Pāti Māori MPs. Labour leader Chris Hipkins agreed that the three MPs broke the rules of Parliament but disagreed with the suspension, instead proposing that Waititi and Ngarewa-Packer be suspended from Parliament for 24 hours and that no further action be taken against Maipi-Clark. Privileges Committee chair Judith Collins defended the suspension, describing their conduct as a "serious incident." [Leader of the House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_House_(New_Zealand) "Leader of the House (New Zealand)")[Chris Bishop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Bishop "Chris Bishop") successfully moved a motion that the suspension debate be deferred until 5 June, allowing the Te Pāti Māori MPs to participate in the upcoming debate around the [2025 New Zealand budget](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_New_Zealand_budget "2025 New Zealand budget"). While the government coalition parties supported Bishop's motion, the opposition parties voted against it.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-89) On 5 June, Parliament voted along party lines to suspend the three TPM MPs.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-90)

#### Green Party–New Zealand First tensions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=54th_New_Zealand_Parliament&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Green Party–New Zealand First tensions")]

On 29 January 2025, the Green Party sent a letter asking Prime Minister [Christopher Luxon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Luxon "Christopher Luxon") and Speaker of the House [Gerry Brownlee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerry_Brownlee "Gerry Brownlee") to condemn alleged racist and xenophobic remarks made by [New Zealand First](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_First "New Zealand First") MPs and government ministers [Winston Peters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winston_Peters "Winston Peters") and [Shane Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Jones "Shane Jones") towards several Green MPs from migrant backgrounds. Jones had made remarks about sending [Mexicans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexicans "Mexicans") home, a reference to Mexican-New Zealander MP [Ricardo Menéndez March](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Men%C3%A9ndez_March "Ricardo Menéndez March") while Peters had accused Green MPs [Lawrence Xu-Nan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_Xu-Nan "Lawrence Xu-Nan") and [Franciso Hernandez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_Hernandez_(politician) "Francisco Hernandez (politician)") of seeking to impose "foreign ideas" on New Zealanders.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-91) In response, Jones and Peters defended their remarks, with the former accusing the aforementioned foreign-born MPs of not respecting New Zealand culture and the latter accusing the Greens of "faux outrage."[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-92) Luxon refused to confirm whether he would discipline Peters and Jones but advised other MPs to "watch their language." The Mexican Embassy to New Zealand said it had raised concerns about Peters and Jones' remarks through diplomatic channels. Peters subsequently confirm that he would meet with the Ambassador at [Waitangi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waitangi,_Northland "Waitangi, Northland") in early February.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-93)

On 19 February 2025, NZ First MPs Peters and Jones criticised Green MP Menéndez March for referring to New Zealand as "[Aotearoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aotearoa "Aotearoa")" while questioning [Immigration Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_Immigration_(New_Zealand) "Minister of Immigration (New Zealand)")[Erica Stanford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erica_Stanford "Erica Stanford"). Peters also sought to change standing orders around references to New Zealand. Speaker Brownlee defended March's right to refer to New Zealand as Aotearoa but reminded MPs to refer to New Zealand by both its [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language "English language") and [Māori language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C4%81ori_language "Māori language") names.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-94) On 4 March, Speaker Brownlee issued a ruling ordering Members of Parliament to stop complaining about the use of Aotearoa as the Māori name for New Zealand.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-95)

On 18 February 2026, Winston Peters twice criticised Green MP [Teanau Tuiono](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teanau_Tuiono "Teanau Tuiono") for referring to New Zealand by its [Māori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C4%81ori_language "Māori language") name [Aotearoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aotearoa "Aotearoa") during a Question Time debate on New Zealand's climate aid policies to the Pacific. In response, Labour leader Chris Hipkins accused Peters of making racist remarks to the ethnic [Cook Islander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cook_Islander "Cook Islander") MP while Speaker Brownlee cautioned Peters against asking unacceptable questions."[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-96) On 19 February, Brownlee ejected Shadow Leader of the House and Labour MP [Kieran McAnulty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kieran_McAnulty "Kieran McAnulty") from a House debate after the latter accused the former of showing "double standards" towards Peters over his treatment of Tuiono.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-97)

On 30 July, Peters told Green MP [Lawrence Xu-Nan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_Xu-Nan "Lawrence Xu-Nan") to "[go back to your own country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Go_back_to_your_own_country "Go back to your own country")" during a debate on the [previous government's response to the COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_government_response_to_the_COVID-19_pandemic "New Zealand government response to the COVID-19 pandemic").[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-98) His remarks drew criticism from other parliamentarians across the spectrum as well as the Chinese Ambassador Wang Xiaoling.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-99)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-100) Prime Minister Luxon condemned Peters' comments as "offensive" but declined to remove his as Foreign Minister.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-101) On 6 August, Speaker Brownlee rejected a Green Party request that Peters to be asked to withdraw and apologise for his remarks towards Xu-Nan.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-102)

#### Chlöe Swarbrick

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=54th_New_Zealand_Parliament&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Chlöe Swarbrick")]

On 12 August 2025, Greens co-leader [Chlöe Swarbrick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chl%C3%B6e_Swarbrick "Chlöe Swarbrick") was removed from Parliament for the rest of the week by Speaker Brownlee after she criticised Government MPs during a debate on the [recognition of Palestine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_recognition_of_Palestine "International recognition of Palestine").[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-103)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-104) The following day, Swarbrick refused to apologise and was "[named](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_(parliamentary_procedure) "Naming (parliamentary procedure)")" by Brownlee, who ordered her to leave Parliament's debating chamber once again. This punishment means that Swarbrick as an MP will have to leave the House of Representatives once again and will have her pay docked for the duration of her suspension.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-105)

On 4 August 2026, Swarbrick was ejected from Parliament after accusing Speaker Brownlee of showing favoritism towards [New Zealand First](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_First "New Zealand First") leader [Winston Peters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winston_Peters "Winston Peters") over opposition Members of Parliament during a Question Time debate. Swarbrick and her Green Party colleagues had also earlier condemned Peters for telling Green MP [Lawrence Xu-Nan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_Xu-Nan "Lawrence Xu-Nan") to "[go back to his own country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Go_back_to_your_own_country "Go back to your own country")" during a parliamentary debate in late July 2026.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-106)

### Dissolution

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=54th_New_Zealand_Parliament&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Dissolution")]

The 54th Parliament will serve until another election is called. Under section 17 of the [Constitution Act 1986](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_Act_1986 "Constitution Act 1986"), Parliament expires three years "from the day fixed for the return of the writs issued for the last preceding general election of members of the House of Representatives, and no longer".[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament#cite_note-Constitution_Act_1986-107) The writ for the [2023 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_New_Zealand_general_election "2023 New Zealand general election") was issued on 10 September 2023 and returned on 16 November 2023, meaning that the 54th Parliament would have to dissolve on or before 16 November 2026.

A general election took place in New Zealand on 14 October 2023 to determine the composition of the 54th New Zealand Parliament. Voters elected 122 members to the unicameral New Zealand House of Representatives under the mixed-member proportional (MMP) voting system, with 71 members elected from single-member electorates and the remaining 51 members elected from closed party lists.[1] Of the 72 electorates, only 71 seats were filled, with the remaining electorate MP determined in the 2023 Port Waikato by-election, due to the death of one of the general election candidates.[b] Two overhang seats were added due to Te Pāti Māori winning six electorate seats when the party vote only entitled them to four seats, with an additional overhang seat added after the National party won the Port Waikato by-election, making for 123 members of parliament.[2]

The incumbent centre-left Labour Party, led by Chris Hipkins, were defeated at the polls, with the centre-right National Party, led by Christopher Luxon, becoming the largest party in the new parliament.[3] The election saw the worst defeat of a sitting government in New Zealand since the introduction of the MMP voting system in 1996, with Labour going from having 65 seats in the first-ever outright majority any party had won under MMP to winning just 34 seats. Labour faced a 23-percentage-point swing against it, failing to mobilise its previous voters in Auckland, especially among young renters or those living in the poorest electorates. National conversely improved its party vote share by 12 points, but returned the second lowest vote share of any party that won the most seats under MMP, the lowest being in 1996. Additionally, Labour and National's combined vote share was the third lowest it had ever been under MMP, and the lowest since 2002. The Green and ACT parties and Te Pāti Maori all increased their vote share, while New Zealand First gained enough votes to return to parliament after being ousted in the 2020 election.

The election had a noticeably turbulent campaign, marked by increased political polarisation and heated disputes over indigenous rights and the theory of co-governance. National made gains in many Auckland electorates that were once considered to be safe Labour seats, such as Mount Roskill and New Lynn, whilst also coming close to winning Jacinda Ardern's former seat of Mount Albert after the left vote was split between Labour and the Greens.[4] The Greens won three electorates, gaining Rongotai and Wellington Central from Labour, while ACT won two electorates, gaining Tāmaki from National. Te Pāti Māori claimed five Māori seats from Labour, which saw 21-year-old Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke become the youngest MP elected in 170 years and in the process unseated incumbent foreign affairs minister Nanaia Mahuta.[5]

Prime Minister Hipkins conceded on election night,[6] paving the way for a National-led government under Christopher Luxon. To form a government, the National Party required support from the ACT Party and New Zealand First.[7] On 24 November 2023, Luxon announced the formation of a coalition government with ACT and New Zealand First.[8] On 27 November 2023, Luxon was sworn in as prime minister by Governor-General Dame Cindy Kiro, thereby marking the end of six years under the Sixth Labour Government and the beginning of the Sixth National Government.[9]

Backgroundedit
Further information: Results of the 2020 New Zealand general election and 53rd New Zealand Parliament

The previous general election held on 17 October 2020 resulted in a majority for the Labour Party, winning 65 seats, allowing them to continue the Sixth Labour Government unrestricted in the 53rd Parliament. Their coalition partner from the 52nd Parliament, New Zealand First, did not receive enough votes to pass the five percent threshold or win in an electorate, removing them from Parliament. Confidence and supply partner the Green Party received 10 seats, up two, becoming the first minor party ever to increase their share of the vote following a term in government. In the opposition, the National Party lost 23 seats, giving them a total of 33, and ACT New Zealand went from one seat to ten. Te Pāti Māori won a Māori electorate and gained an additional list seat, returning to Parliament after a one-term absence, having lost all seats in the 2017 election.[10]

In the 2022 Tauranga by-election, National retained the marginal seat with a large swing away from Labour.[11] In the 2022 Hamilton West by-election, National gained the seat from Labour.[12]

Since the previous election, the leadership of both the Labour and National parties changed. Christopher Luxon replaced Judith Collins as National leader on 30 November 2021.[13] Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern announced her resignation on 19 January 2023 and was succeeded later that month by education minister Chris Hipkins.[14]

Electoral systemedit
Main article: Electoral system of New Zealand

New Zealand uses a mixed-member proportional (MMP) voting system to elect the 120 members of the House of Representatives.[15] Each voter gets two votes: one for a political party (the party vote) and one for a local candidate (the electorate vote). Political parties that meet the threshold (5% of the party vote or one electorate seat) receive seats in the House in proportion to the share of the party vote they receive.

72 of the 120 seats are filled by the MPs elected from the electorates, with the winner in each electorate determined by the first-past-the-post method (i.e. the candidate with the most votes wins). Electorate boundaries for the election were the same as for the 2020 election, with 65 general electorates (49 in the North Island and 16 in the South Island) and 7 Māori electorates. Boundaries are due to be redrawn in 2024, after the 2023 census.[16]

The remaining 48 seats are filled by candidates from each party's closed party list.[17] If a party wins more electorates than seats it is entitled to under the party vote, an overhang seat occurs; in that case, the party winning overhang seats keeps that many extra seats in addition to the 120 seats distributed proportionally.[18]

New Zealand electoral law also allows for an overhang seat to be created if a candidate dies between the opening and closing of the vote. In 2023, this occurred for the first time since the adoption of MMP (indeed, since 1957).[19] The ACT candidate for Port Waikato, Neil Christensen, died on 9 October. As a result, the electorate vote was required to be cancelled in the electorate, and a by-election was scheduled for November, after the general election, to determine the MP for Port Waikato. Voters in Port Waikato continued to cast party votes in the general election. Electoral law requires that 120 seats, excluding overhang, are filled proportionally through the general election. Therefore the electoral system provided for a 49th list MP to be elected through the general election and a 121st MP (excluding other overhang seats) through the Port Waikato by-election.

The political party or party bloc with the majority of the seats in the House forms the government. Since the introduction of MMP in 1996, no party had won enough votes to win an outright majority of seats until the landslide 2020 Labour victory, which gave them 65 seats. When no party has commanded a majority, parties have had to negotiate with other parties to form a coalition government or a minority government.[20]

With 123 seats (because of the Port Waikato overhang and the overhang seats awarded to Te Pāti Māori), a party, coalition, or minority government with confidence and supply support requires 62 seats for a majority. The last time an overhang this large, three additional seats in Parliament, occurred was in 2008.

Election date and scheduleedit

Unless an early election is called or the election date is set to circumvent holding a by-election, a general election is held every three years.[21] The previous election was held on 17 October 2020.

The governor-general, Dame Cindy Kiro, signs the writ for the general election at Government House, Auckland, on 10 September 2023, watched by the chief electoral officer, Karl Le Quesne.

The governor-general must issue writs for an election within seven days of the expiration or dissolution of the current parliament. Under section 17 of the Constitution Act 1986, parliament expires three years "from the day fixed for the return of the writs issued for the last preceding general election of members of the House of Representatives, and no longer." The writs for the 2020 election were returned on 20 November 2020;[22] as a result, the 53rd Parliament had to dissolve no later than 20 November 2023. Writs must be issued within seven days,[23] so the last day for issuance of the writs was 27 November 2023. Writs must be returned within 60 days of their issuance (save for any judicial recount, death of a candidate, or emergency adjournment),[24] which would be 26 January 2024. Because polling day must be a Saturday,[24] and ten days is required for the counting of special votes,[25] the latest possible date that this election could have been held is 13 January 2024.[26] However, it was widely accepted by political commentators, news media and the Electoral Commission that the next election would be held in late 2023.[27][28][29][30][31][32] News website Stuff, as part of its annual political predictions, predicted that the election would be in November so as not to coincide with the New Zealand co-hosted 2023 FIFA Women's World Cup, which finishes in August, and the 2023 Men's Rugby World Cup, which finishes in October.[33]

On 19 January 2023, Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern announced Saturday 14 October 2023 as the election date.[34] The indicative schedule for the election is as follows:[35]

On 30 August 2023, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced in Adelaide that the 2023 Australian Indigenous Voice referendum would be held on 14 October 2023. This means that tens of thousands of New Zealand Australians would be voting in two polls on the same day.[38][39] Some have suggested that the referendum may have an impact on Māori issues in the New Zealand election.[38][39] Australia has the largest number of New Zealand expats in the world, with 530,491 New Zealand-born people living in Australia as of the 2021 Australian census, making up 2.1% of Australia's total population.[40]

Partiesedit

Political parties registered with the Electoral Commission can contest the general election as a party. To register, parties must have at least 500 financial members, an auditor, and an appropriate party name.[41] A registered party may submit a party list to contest the party vote, and can have a party campaign expenses limit in addition to limits on individual candidates' campaigns. Unregistered parties and independents can contest the electorate vote only.[42]

Since the 2020 election, six parties have been deregistered: Mana on 5 May 2021,[43] Advance New Zealand on 19 August 2021,[44] Sustainable NZ on 15 December 2021,[45] New Zealand TEA Party on 21 September 2022,[46] New Zealand Social Credit Party on 28 February 2023,[47] and Heartland New Zealand on 22 June 2023.[48]

Fundraisingedit

On 18 January 2023, The New Zealand Herald reported that the National Party had raised NZ$2.3 million from 24 big donors while the ACT Party had raised NZ$1.1 million in large donations in 2022 to fund their 2023 election campaigns. By comparison, the incumbent Labour Party had raised $150,000, the Greens ($122,000) and New Zealand First ($35,000) during that same period.[70] By 23 June, ACT had raised a further $1.15 million in big donations, followed by National (about $700,000), New Zealand First ($517,000), the Greens (about $500,000), and Labour ($458,000).[71]

By 14 September, Radio New Zealand reported that National had received $1.1 million, ACT ($375,000), the Greens ($100,000), and NZ First ($50,000) in business donations between early 2021 and September 2023. During the same period, Labour had received about $600,000 in large donations from unions and individuals but no significant business donations. An interim report published by the Independent Electoral Review has recommended limiting political donations to individuals, and banning businesses and unions from donating to parties. Review member Professor Andrew Geddis expressed concern about banning businesses from donating to parties but allowing unions to donate.[72]

On 29 July 2024, Radio New Zealand reported that the National, Labour, ACT, Green, New Zealand First parties and Te Pāti Māori had received a total of almost NZ$25 million in donations during the 2023 general election, the biggest total declared in New Zealand history and three times the amount declared during the 2017 New Zealand general election. Economist Max Rashbrooke has argued that businesses and unions should not be allowed to donate to political parties and urged New Zealand to follow Canada and several European countries in limiting donations to registered voters.[73]

Campaigningedit
Expense limits and broadcasting allocationsedit
Parties and candidatesedit

During the regulated period prior to election day, parties and candidates have limits on how much they may spend on election campaigning. The limits are updated every year to reflect inflation. It is illegal in New Zealand to campaign on election day itself, or within 10 metres of an advance polling booth.[76]

For the 2023 general election, every registered party contending the party vote is permitted to spend $1,388,000 plus $32,600 per electorate candidate on campaigning during the regulated period, excluding radio and television campaigning (broadcasting funding is allocated separately). For example, a registered party with candidates in all 72 electorates is permitted to spend $3,735,200 on campaigning for the party vote. Electorate candidates are permitted to spend $32,600 each on campaigning for the electorate vote.[77]

Broadcasting allocationedit

Registered parties are allocated a separate broadcasting budget for radio and television campaigning. Only money from the broadcasting allocation can be used to purchase airtime; production costs can come from the general election expenses budget. The Electoral Commission determines how much broadcasting funding each party gets, set out by part 6 of the Broadcasting Act 1989. The allocation is based a number of factors including the number of seats in the current Parliament, results of the previous general election and any by-elections since, and support in opinion polls.[78]

An initial broadcasting allocation was released from the Electoral Commission on 12 May 2023.[79] On 31 May Freedoms New Zealand and two of its component parties, the NZ Outdoors & Freedom Party and Vision New Zealand, challenged the Electoral Commission's decision to allocate broadcasting funds to them collectively rather than as individual political parties. The Electoral Commission had decided to allocate broadcasting funds to them collectively on the basis that they were a "group of parties" that had joined forces. The plaintiffs argued that the Broadcasting Act 1989 did not clearly define what was a "group of parties" and that the Electoral Commission had not published clear criteria for how their parties had joined forces.[80] On 17 July 2023, the High Court dismissed the case.[81]

The final broadcasting allocation was released on 8 September 2023.[82] For comparison, the cost of a 30-second television slot in October 2023 ranged from $250 during the daytime to over $29,000 on TVNZ 1 during 1 News at 6pm and Country Calendar.[83][84][85]
